title: When do you use `MERGE` vs `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` (MERGE supports matched/not-matched/delete branches for complex ETL; ON CONFLICT is simpler for single-row upserts), and what is the gotcha with upsert + auto-increment (sequence gaps on conflict)?
shortTitle: MERGE Versus INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, and the Auto-Increment Gotcha
topicTitle: SQL Basics — SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY

s1_definition.profdef: `MERGE` is the SQL-standard statement that compares a target table against a source and runs different actions per row — `WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE`, `WHEN MATCHED THEN DELETE`, and `WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT` — making it ideal for complex ETL that must insert, update, and delete in one pass. `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` is a simpler, more focused upsert for the common insert-or-update of individual rows. The auto-increment gotcha is that an upsert whose insert path conflicts may still have consumed a sequence or auto-increment value before the conflict was detected, leaving a gap in the generated identifiers, which is expected behaviour.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of reconciling National Bank of India's account master against a nightly feed from a partner bank. MERGE is the full reconciliation clerk: for each incoming record, update if the account exists, insert if it is new, and delete if the feed says the account closed — all in one controlled pass. INSERT ON CONFLICT is the simpler clerk who only ever says "add this, or if it already exists, update it." The gotcha is that every time the simple clerk tries to add a row with a new ticket number from the ticket machine, that ticket is spent even if the add turns into an update, so the ticket numbers develop harmless gaps.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use MERGE for multi-action ETL (insert/update/delete in one pass); use INSERT ON CONFLICT for simple single-row upserts — and expect sequence gaps because the auto-increment is consumed before a conflict is detected.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `MERGE` is the SQL-standard statement that compares a target table against a source and runs different actions per row — `WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE`, `WHEN MATCHED THEN DELETE`, and `WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT` — making it ideal for complex ETL that must insert, update, and delete in one pass. `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` is a simpler, more focused upsert for the common insert-or-update of individual rows. The auto-increment gotcha is that an upsert whose insert path conflicts may still have consumed a sequence or auto-increment value before the conflict was detected, leaving a gap in the generated identifiers, which is expected behaviour.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of reconciling National Bank of India's account master against a nightly feed from a partner bank. MERGE is the full reconciliation clerk: for each incoming record, update if the account exists, insert if it is new, and delete if the feed says the account closed — all in one controlled pass. INSERT ON CONFLICT is the simpler clerk who only ever says "add this, or if it already exists, update it." The gotcha is that every time the simple clerk tries to add a row with a new ticket number from the ticket machine, that ticket is spent even if the add turns into an update, so the ticket numbers develop harmless gaps.

**One line to remember:** Use MERGE for multi-action ETL (insert/update/delete in one pass); use INSERT ON CONFLICT for simple single-row upserts — and expect sequence gaps because the auto-increment is consumed before a conflict is detected.

sections.s2_technical:
MERGE takes a target table and a source (a table, a subquery, or a VALUES list), joins them on a condition, and for each resulting row chooses an action based on whether it matched. WHEN MATCHED can UPDATE or DELETE; WHEN NOT MATCHED can INSERT; and you can have several WHEN branches with extra conditions, such as WHEN MATCHED AND status equals CLOSED THEN DELETE. This expressiveness makes MERGE the tool for ETL where a single batch must apply inserts, updates, and deletes derived from a source feed, in one atomic statement, with one pass over the data.

INSERT ... ON CONFLICT is narrower by design. It handles the frequent case of "insert this row, but if it collides on a unique key, update it (or do nothing)." It is simpler to read, has fewer sharp edges, and is the natural choice for single-row or small-batch upserts from application code. It cannot delete and does not express multiple conditional branches the way MERGE does.

Choosing between them: reach for MERGE when the operation is genuinely multi-action — the source implies some rows must be inserted, some updated, and some deleted — or for set-based ETL reconciliations. Reach for ON CONFLICT (or MySQL's ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE) when you just need an idempotent insert-or-update of a row. A further consideration is historical: MERGE arrived in PostgreSQL only in version 15, and its early implementations in various databases had concurrency quirks, so for a plain concurrent upsert ON CONFLICT is often the safer, battle-tested pick.

The auto-increment gotcha applies to both. When a table has a serial or identity column backed by a sequence, the engine typically draws the next sequence value as part of attempting the insert, before it discovers the unique-key conflict that diverts the row into the update branch. Sequences are non-transactional by design — they do not roll back — so that drawn value is simply gone, leaving a gap in the identifiers. The same happens on any rolled-back insert. This is normal and intentional: sequences guarantee uniqueness and monotonicity, not gaplessness. The practical lesson is never to assume generated IDs are contiguous, and never to use "max ID" as a count.

The senior nuance is that if you truly need gapless numbers — for a legally sequential invoice series, say — you do not use a bare sequence; you use a dedicated counter row updated inside the transaction, accepting the contention that creates, or a separate numbering step that handles gaps deliberately.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: National Bank of India reconciles its account-status table against a nightly partner feed. New accounts must be inserted, changed accounts updated, and closed accounts deleted — a perfect MERGE. Separately, a simple daily-balance upsert uses ON CONFLICT, and we want to observe sequence gaps.

Problem 1 — multi-action reconciliation. We model a MERGE that, for each feed row, updates matched active accounts, deletes matched closed ones, and inserts brand-new ones, in one pass.

Problem 2 — simple single-row upsert. We model INSERT ON CONFLICT for the daily balance to contrast the simpler case.

Problem 3 — the sequence gap. We model an identity sequence that is incremented on every insert attempt, so a conflicting upsert still burns a number, producing a visible gap.

The code includes a MergeEngine that applies matched/not-matched/delete branches, an UpsertEngine with a sequence that gaps on conflict, and a demo running both.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql (Flyway)
CREATE TABLE account_status (
    account_id VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    status     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL          -- ACTIVE / CLOSED
);
CREATE TABLE daily_balance (
    id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,          -- sequence-backed → can gap
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    day        DATE NOT NULL,
    balance    DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    UNIQUE (account_id, day)
);

-- MERGE (PG15+): reconcile account_status against a partner feed
-- MERGE INTO account_status t USING partner_feed s ON t.account_id = s.account_id
--   WHEN MATCHED AND s.status='CLOSED' THEN DELETE
--   WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET status = s.status
--   WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (account_id, status) VALUES (s.account_id, s.status);

-- Simple upsert (ON CONFLICT) — note BIGSERIAL id may gap on conflict:
-- INSERT INTO daily_balance (account_id, day, balance) VALUES ('SAV2001', CURRENT_DATE, 950000)
--   ON CONFLICT (account_id, day) DO UPDATE SET balance = EXCLUDED.balance;
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
etl:
  reconcile-cron: "0 0 1 * * *"   # 1 AM nightly reconciliation
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: an account-status table and a nightly feed, plus a series of daily-balance upserts.

Step 1 — The MERGE processes the feed in one pass. SAV2001 exists and the feed says SUSPENDED, so the WHEN MATCHED branch updates its status. OLD9999 exists and the feed says CLOSED, so the WHEN MATCHED AND CLOSED branch deletes it. CUR3001 is not in the target, so the WHEN NOT MATCHED branch inserts it. One statement did an update, a delete, and an insert.

Step 2 — The resulting account-status table has SAV2001 suspended, CUR3001 active, and OLD9999 gone — exactly the reconciliation outcome.

Step 3 — The ON CONFLICT upserts run. The first two keys are new and get ids 1 and 2. The third upsert reuses the SAV2001 key, so the sequence first draws id 3 — then the conflict is detected and the row is updated instead, wasting id 3.

Step 4 — The fourth upsert is a new key and gets id 4. The ids actually stored are 1, 2, and 4; id 3 is a permanent gap because sequences do not roll back. This demonstrates the auto-increment gotcha.

Final output:

```
2026-10-25 17:40:00 [INFO] === MERGE: reconcile account_status against nightly feed ===
2026-10-25 17:40:00 [INFO] WHEN MATCHED → UPDATE SAV2001=SUSPENDED
2026-10-25 17:40:00 [INFO] WHEN MATCHED + CLOSED → DELETE OLD9999
2026-10-25 17:40:00 [INFO] WHEN NOT MATCHED → INSERT CUR3001=ACTIVE
2026-10-25 17:40:00 [INFO] account_status after MERGE = {SAV2001=SUSPENDED, CUR3001=ACTIVE}
2026-10-25 17:40:00 [INFO] === ON CONFLICT upsert: watch the sequence gap ===
2026-10-25 17:40:00 [INFO] INSERT SAV2001|2026-10-25 id=1
2026-10-25 17:40:00 [INFO] INSERT CUR3001|2026-10-25 id=2
2026-10-25 17:40:00 [WARNING] CONFLICT on SAV2001|2026-10-25 → UPDATE existing id=1; sequence value 3 WASTED (gap)
2026-10-25 17:40:00 [INFO] INSERT NEW5005|2026-10-25 id=4
2026-10-25 17:40:00 [INFO] last sequence value = 4 (ids used: 1,2,4; 3 is a gap)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Nightly partner feed                    Daily-balance upserts
    │                                       │
    ▼                                       ▼
  MERGE INTO account_status USING feed    INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (account,day)
    ├─ MATCHED           → UPDATE         │  draw next sequence id
    ├─ MATCHED + CLOSED  → DELETE         ├─ no conflict → INSERT (id kept)
    └─ NOT MATCHED       → INSERT         └─ conflict    → UPDATE (id WASTED → gap)
    ▼                                       ▼
  reconciled status table                 ids: 1,2,4  (3 missing = harmless gap)
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — MERGE vs ON CONFLICT ═══

  ┌─ Patterns ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  MERGE: rule branches (matched/not-matched/delete)         │
  │  ON CONFLICT: focused idempotent single-row upsert         │
  │  Sequence: non-transactional counter (gaps on conflict)    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─ SOLID ───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: MergeEngine reconciles; UpsertEngine upserts.          │
  │  O: new MERGE branch = new condition, engine unchanged.    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ MergeEngine              │   │ UpsertEngine             │
  │ + merge(target, source)  │   │ - sequence: AtomicLong   │
  │   matched→update/delete  │   │ + upsert(key): long      │
  │   not-matched→insert     │   │   (gaps id on conflict)  │
  └──────────────────────────┘   └──────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. merge(target, feed) → UPDATE SAV2001, DELETE OLD9999, INSERT CUR3001
  2. upsert ×4 → ids 1,2,(3 wasted),4 → gap at 3
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
MERGE is the SQL-standard statement that compares a target table against a source and runs a different action per row — WHEN MATCHED it can UPDATE or DELETE, and WHEN NOT MATCHED it can INSERT, with extra conditions allowed on each branch. That makes it the right tool for complex ETL where a single batch derived from a source feed must insert some rows, update others, and delete others, all in one atomic pass over the data. INSERT with ON CONFLICT is deliberately narrower: it handles the common case of insert-this-row-but-update-it-if-it-collides on a unique key, it is simpler to read, and it is the natural choice for single-row or small-batch upserts from application code. It cannot delete and does not express multiple conditional branches.

So I choose MERGE when the operation is genuinely multi-action — a reconciliation where the source implies inserts, updates, and deletes together — and I choose ON CONFLICT, or MySQL's ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, when I just need an idempotent single-row upsert. I also keep in mind that MERGE only arrived in PostgreSQL 15 and had some early concurrency quirks across databases, so for a plain concurrent upsert the battle-tested ON CONFLICT is often the safer pick.

The gotcha that both share is with auto-increment and sequences. When a table has a serial or identity column, the engine draws the next sequence value as part of attempting the insert, before it discovers the unique-key conflict that diverts the row into the update branch. Sequences are non-transactional and never roll back, so that drawn value is simply lost, leaving a permanent gap in the identifiers. In our National Bank of India daily-balance table we saw ids jump from two to four because a conflicting upsert burned id three — and that is perfectly normal, because a sequence guarantees uniqueness and monotonicity, not gaplessness. The practical rules I follow are to never assume generated ids are contiguous and never treat the maximum id as a row count, and when I genuinely need a gapless series like a legal invoice number, I use a dedicated counter row updated inside the transaction instead of a bare sequence. The line I remember is to use MERGE for multi-action ETL and INSERT ON CONFLICT for simple single-row upserts, and to expect sequence gaps because the auto-increment is consumed before the conflict is ever detected.
